name: Movember

card.summary: An annual November moustache-growing charity month that gives people a reason to try facial hair, with grooming as part of the fun.
card.note: Charity campaign with an appearance side effect rather than a looks treatment.

quick.overview:
Movember is a yearly event in which men grow a moustache through November to raise money and awareness for men's health: prostate and testicular cancer, and mental health and suicide prevention. Participants are called Mo Bros.

Its appearance angle is the moustache itself, a month-long trial of facial hair that many people use to see how it suits their face and to experiment with shaping and grooming.
quick.how: Participants register, start the month clean shaven, grow a moustache and collect donations. Groups run team competitions and some add grooming steps such as trimming, shaping and beard oil.
quick.risks: Risks are minimal and cosmetic, such as skin irritation from growth and trimming. Critics in the medical literature have questioned how the campaign's messages on screening are framed.

lead: Movember is an annual November event in which participants grow moustaches to raise awareness of men's health and funds for charity. It is run by the Movember Foundation, headquartered in Melbourne, and its cause areas are prostate cancer, testicular cancer, and mental health and suicide prevention [1][2]. The name blends "moustache" and "November", and participants are called Mo Bros, with supporters sometimes called Mo Sistas [1][2].

For people interested in appearance, Movember works as a time-limited facial hair experiment. Participants begin the month clean shaven, let a moustache grow for thirty days and shape it as they go, which gives many a low-commitment way to see how a moustache or other facial hair suits their face. Some keep or change their style afterwards [1].

The campaign is among the best-known awareness events in the world. Wikipedia reports that 1.1 million people signed up in 2012 and raised about 95 million dollars, and the foundation has since funded large research and mental health programmes [2][3]. It has also been examined in the medical literature, including a 2012 BMJ analysis questioning its screening messages, and studies of the research agendas the foundation sponsors [4][5].

angle.text: Movember motivates a month of moustache growth that can reveal how a moustache or other facial hair looks on a given face. The campaign's purpose is charity, with grooming as a visible byproduct.

paras: Participants register, begin November clean shaven, grow a moustache and seek sponsorship from friends, family and colleagues. The foundation also encourages men to have check-ups, learn their family medical history and adopt healthier habits [2]. Teams, workplaces and sports clubs often compete on fundraising, and the moustache serves as a conversation starter about topics men may otherwise avoid [1][2].

Women and others who do not grow a moustache take part as Mo Sistas or through other activities such as challenges and fundraising events [1]. Grokipedia notes that the foundation has had to adapt in places where moustache growth is limited by genetics or where moustaches carry particular cultural associations, offering other ways to take part [1].

Wikipedia traces the idea to a 1999 Adelaide news segment about young men who coined the name and grew moustaches for charity, raising money for the RSPCA through T-shirt sales [2]. The Movember Foundation's own story, as summarised by Grokipedia, begins in Melbourne when friends Travis Garone and Luke Slattery joked about reviving the moustache trend; they challenged about 30 friends to grow one and later added a charitable aim after being inspired by a breast cancer fundraiser [1].

Wikipedia dates the Melbourne event to 2004, when Adam Garone, Travis Garone, Luke Slattery and Justin Coghlan started what became the foundation. In the following year nearly 500 participants raised over 40,000 dollars for the Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia [2]. Grokipedia gives figures of 450 registrations and 54,000 Australian dollars for 2004; the two accounts differ in some details [1][2].

The event spread to New Zealand and then, in 2007, to countries including Ireland, Canada, the United Kingdom, Spain and the United States; Wikipedia records U.S. charity status in 2009 [2]. In 2010 Movember merged with the testicular cancer event Tacheback, and it launched the Moscars video contest and the International Man of Movember title, with national winners from 2010 onwards [2]. The Global Journal listed it among the world's top 100 NGOs in 2012 [2].

Movember's visual identity is the moustache, and participants commonly photograph their progress, post it to social media and share styles. The month acts as a collective excuse to try styles that people might not otherwise wear to work or school, and brands have joined in. Wikipedia lists corporate partners such as Google Chrome, TOMS, Qantas, Royal Mail and Pringles, and appearances in video games including Football Manager 2015 and FIFA, with athletes and celebrities such as Kevin Love and Valtteri Bottas supporting the cause [2].

Similar events exist in other settings. Wikipedia lists Mustache March in the U.S. Air Force, Novembro Azul in Brazil and Decembeard, a facial hair event focused on bowel cancer awareness [2]. Practitioners' grooming choices within the month, such as trimming, shaping and using beard oil, are matters of personal routine rather than anything the campaign prescribes.

A 2012 BMJ analysis argued that Movember's emphasis on screening tests rested on recommendations about testing frequency that were not evidence-based, and that mental illness, substance misuse, smoking and obesity received limited attention in its messaging [4][2]. Two 2015 studies of Twitter activity, cited on Wikipedia, found that online conversation focused mostly on the social side of the campaign, with little discussion of health and almost none of mental health [2].

The foundation also funds research. A 2020 landscape analysis commissioned by Movember, with a committee of experts and input from men with prostate cancer, agreed 17 research needs, of which three received the top score, including more sensitive and specific tests for screening and diagnosis [5]. Later Movember-convened consensus work addressed active surveillance for low-risk prostate cancer [6]. Researchers have also described a tool, Check-Mate, developed within the foundation's Social Innovators Challenge to help men's mental health programmes address gender-related influences [7]. Editorials in medical journals have noted the campaign's reach [8][9].
No studies found on Movember as an appearance practice. Medical papers concern the campaign's messaging and the research and programmes it funds [4][5][7].

Melbourne friends' moustache challenge begins, per the foundation's story as summarised by Grokipedia [1].
